output.title: Firmware 1.4.2 associated with a large rise in BLE disconnects per device-day
output.summary: The leading hypothesis attributes the 1.4.2 BLE disconnect spike to a documented supervisor-timeout/backoff change. A falsifying test is proposed: hold phone OS/model constant across 1.4.2 and 1.4.1 and re-run the comparison, ideally under controlled outdoor/body-block RF conditions; if the rate-ratio confidence interval then includes one, the firmware-timing mechanism is falsified in favor of a device/OS-side confound analogous to INC-2025-014. An additional check on the internal_dogfood cohort shows the elevated ratio persists there as well, which weakens but does not eliminate the phone-OS alternative, since phone OS/model itself was never directly queried.

leading_hypothesis.statement: Firmware 1.4.2's supervisor-timeout reduction and shortened retry backoff (documented in KD-02) is associated with a substantially higher measured BLE disconnect rate relative to 1.4.1, holding app version and region constant.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: The elevated disconnect rate on firmware 1.4.2 reflects a phone-OS/Bluetooth-stack confound (as in INC-2025-014) rather than the supervisor-timeout/backoff change itself, e.g. because the 1.4.2 rollout wave is disproportionately paired with certain phone models or OS versions not controlled for in this investigation.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Hold phone OS/model constant (not just app version and region) and compare 1.4.2 vs 1.4.1 disconnect rates; if the elevated ratio persists with the CI still excluding one after phone OS/model is held fixed, this alternative is rejected, but if the ratio's CI includes one once phone OS/model is fixed, the leading firmware-timing hypothesis is falsified.

Total BLE disconnect events, firmware 1.4.2, current window

supporting_evidence.claim: 1.4.2 devices show a disconnect rate roughly seven times that of 1.4.1 devices in the current window, with the rate-ratio CI excluding one, per {f_3}.
Both the 1.4.1 cohort ({f_6}) and 1.4.2 cohort ({f_5}) in the current window are entirely on app version 3.2, so the gap is not explained by app version.
1.4.2 disconnect rates are uniform across benelux, dach, iberia, nordics, and uk regions, arguing against a regional driver.

Firmware 1.4.2 release notes document a supervision-timeout reduction and a shortened exponential retry backoff cap, intended for faster drop detection, with outdoor/body-block/commuting RF explicitly not re-characterized after the change.

counter_evidence.claim: Lab soak testing for 1.4.2, conducted on a small indoor-office fleet, showed link-loss counts in the same band as 1.4.1, so the lab environment did not reproduce the field-scale increase.

A prior firmware-timing hypothesis for a disconnect cluster (1.3.0, INC-2025-014) was later overturned in favor of a phone-OS Bluetooth stack cause, illustrating that a firmware release note coinciding with a disconnect cluster is not by itself proof of firmware causation.

The elevated 1.4.2 vs 1.4.1 disconnect-rate ratio, with its confidence interval excluding one, also holds within the internal_dogfood cohort alone, which is the cohort most likely to have controlled or known phone models; this weakens (but does not eliminate, since phone OS/model was still not directly checked) the alternative phone-OS confound explanation.

Lab soak testing for 1.4.2 (indoor-office fleet) did not reproduce the field-scale elevated link-loss rate, indicating the documented supervisor-timing change alone, absent outdoor/body-block/commuting RF exposure, may be insufficient to explain the field magnitude.

recommended_actions.description: Run a controlled RF characterization for firmware 1.4.2 (outdoor, body-block, commuting conditions) to test whether the shortened supervision timeout and retry backoff reproduce the field-scale disconnect increase seen in telemetry.
Attempt to split phone OS/model from firmware train for a subset of 1.4.2 devices, mirroring the INC-2025-014 methodology, before attributing the disconnect rise solely to firmware.
Flag firmware 1.4.2's BLE supervisor-timing change as a candidate rollback/hotfix target pending the RF characterization results.

uncertainty: No controlled outdoor/body-block/commuting RF test has been run for 1.4.2; lab soak (indoor only) did not show the elevated rate seen in the field, leaving a gap between documented intent and observed field behavior.
Phone OS/model was not held constant in this investigation, so a phone-side confound analogous to INC-2025-014 has not been excluded.

The severity/affected_cohort figures are carried over from triage and have not been independently re-derived from device-level session outcomes (e.g., whether faster reconnection offsets user-visible impact).

Phone OS/model has still not been directly queried or held constant in any comparison performed so far, including the dogfood-cohort check, so the phone-side confound from INC-2025-014 is weakened but not formally excluded.

No controlled outdoor/body-block/commuting RF test has been run for 1.4.2 vs 1.4.1; the indoor lab soak did not reproduce the field effect, leaving the causal mechanism (RF environment interacting with shortened timeout/backoff) unconfirmed.

The persistence of the elevated ratio within the internal_dogfood cohort is itself only correlational and could still reflect a device-mix or environment-mix difference within that small cohort rather than firmware mechanism.

output.title: Overheating-tagged feedback cluster traced to known cosmetic app-UI issue, not a thermal event
output.summary: The leading hypothesis (overheating tickets = misread battery UI chrome, KI-UI-011) rests on a small ticket sample and aggregate skin_temp_delta_c trend. A direct falsifying test is to check the full 'overheating' ticket set for any records that both lack the 'battery'/'app-ui' co-tags and describe genuine device heat rather than battery drain/red-screen confusion; finding even a modest number of such records would falsify the claim that the entire cluster is explained by the cosmetic UI issue. A follow-up query for heat-specific language among overheating-tagged tickets returned no matches, and regional skin_temp_delta_c rates are flat across all regions, neither confirming nor ruling out a residual thermal subpopulation, so status remains NOT_AN_INCIDENT but with the falsifying test left open for a fuller ticket-population check.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The 'overheating' tag cluster reflects users misreading the app's red low-battery UI chrome (KI-UI-011, accepted cosmetic UX debt) during cold-weather battery drain, rather than an actual thermal or device-heat event.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A subset of 'overheating' tagged tickets may reflect genuine localized device heat (e.g., during charging or high motion_intensity periods) that is independent of the KI-UI-011 battery-chrome misread, and is masked when the whole tag cluster is treated as one cause.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Pull the full (not sampled) set of current-window 'overheating' tickets and check whether any lack the co-occurring 'battery' and 'app-ui' tags, or whether ticket text reports device heat without any battery-drain/red-screen language and without a charging context; the leading hypothesis cannot be true if such non-overlapping, genuinely-thermal tickets exist in nontrivial number.

supporting_evidence.claim: Every sampled current-window 'overheating' ticket also carries 'battery' and 'app-ui' tags, and text describes cold-weather battery drain and an alarming sync/battery screen rather than a hot device.
The same co-occurrence pattern (overheating with battery and app-ui, identical tag counts) held in the prior window.

A known issue register entry (KI-UI-011) documents that the app's battery chrome renders a harsh red fill below a low-charge threshold that reads as an overheating warning, and is accepted cosmetic UX debt.

The knowledge base states skin_temp_delta_c is a patch-site delta, not ambient temperature, and its correlation with battery_drain_pct on Nordics device-days is about zero, so it should not be used to argue a thermal cause for battery-drain complaints.

counter_evidence.claim: skin_temp_delta_c did decline slightly rather than staying perfectly flat, which is directionally consistent with the falling trend in ticket volume but too small a movement to establish a thermal mechanism either way.

A targeted re-query for 'overheating'-tagged tickets in the current window matching heat-related terms returned zero matched records, so the earlier small sample cannot be confirmed to represent the full tag cluster; the full-population co-occurrence with 'battery' and 'app-ui' has not actually been verified end-to-end.

skin_temp_delta_c broken down by region in the current window is essentially uniform across benelux, dach, iberia, nordics, and uk, showing no region-specific thermal signal that would either support or rule out a localized heat event underlying some overheating reports.

leading_hypothesis.statement: The 'overheating' tag cluster reflects users misreading the app's red low-battery UI chrome (KI-UI-011, accepted cosmetic UX debt) during cold-weather battery drain, rather than an actual thermal or device-heat event.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: Devices are genuinely running hot (patch-site or ambient) and this is being flagged correctly as a hardware thermal issue.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Check whether skin_temp_delta_c rises alongside overheating-tagged tickets and whether it correlates with battery_drain_pct on affected device-days; both are flat/near-zero here.

alternative_hypotheses.statement: A firmware or app version regression is independently driving both battery drain and overheating perception.
alternative_hypotheses.falsifying_test: Run compare_versions on battery_drain_pct and skin_temp_delta_c across firmware_version/app_version to check for a version-specific step change coincident with the ticket cluster.

supporting_evidence.claim: Every sampled current-window 'overheating' ticket also carries 'battery' and 'app-ui' tags, and text describes cold-weather battery drain and an alarming sync/battery screen rather than a hot device.
The same co-occurrence pattern (overheating with battery and app-ui, identical tag counts) held in the prior window.

A known issue register entry (KI-UI-011) documents that the app's battery chrome renders a harsh red fill below a low-charge threshold that reads as an overheating warning, and is accepted cosmetic UX debt.

The knowledge base states skin_temp_delta_c is a patch-site delta, not ambient temperature, and its correlation with battery_drain_pct on Nordics device-days is about zero, so it should not be used to argue a thermal cause for battery-drain complaints.

counter_evidence.claim: skin_temp_delta_c did decline slightly rather than staying perfectly flat, which is directionally consistent with the falling trend in ticket volume but too small a movement to establish a thermal mechanism either way.

recommended_actions.description: Tag this ticket cluster as a duplicate of KI-UI-011 in the support queue so agents route it as a known cosmetic UI issue rather than escalating as a thermal safety concern.

Continue monitoring skin_temp_delta_c and battery_drain_pct trends by region for any future divergence that would indicate a genuine, non-cosmetic shift, rather than closing the metric watch entirely.

uncertainty: Only a small sample of matched tickets was inspected per window; the full set was not reviewed for outliers that might describe a genuinely hot device.
No breakdown by firmware or app version was run to rule out a version-specific contributor to the battery-drain-driven UI warning.
